claim: Mutations in B3GNT1 are causal for congenital muscular dystrophy with hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan (secondary dystroglycanopathies).
source: Recent studies demonstrated that mutations in B3GNT1, an enzyme proposed to be involved in poly-N-acetyllactosamine synthesis, were causal for congenital muscular dystrophy with hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan (secondary dystroglycanopathies).
evidence: Supported by references to recent studies in the abstract

claim: B3GNT1 was proposed to be involved in poly-N-acetyllactosamine synthesis.
source: Recent studies demonstrated that mutations in B3GNT1, an enzyme proposed to be involved in poly-N-acetyllactosamine synthesis, were causal for congenital muscular dystrophy with hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan (secondary dystroglycanopathies).
evidence: Refers to prior characterization of B3GNT1 in the literature

claim: No established O-mannose initiated structures containing a β3 linked GlcNAc are known.
source: Since defects in the O-mannosylation protein glycosylation pathway are primarily responsible for dystroglycanopathies and with no established O-mannose initiated structures containing a β3 linked GlcNAc known, we biochemically interrogated this human enzyme.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: B3GNT1 is not a β-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase with catalytic activity towards β-galactose.
source: Here we report this enzyme is not a β-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase with catalytic activity towards β-galactose but rather a β-1,4-glucuronyltransferase, designated B4GAT1, towards both α- and β-anomers of xylose.
evidence: Experimental findings reported in the manuscript

claim: B3GNT1 is a β-1,4-glucuronyltransferase, designated B4GAT1, towards both α- and β-anomers of xylose.
source: Here we report this enzyme is not a β-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase with catalytic activity towards β-galactose but rather a β-1,4-glucuronyltransferase, designated B4GAT1, towards both α- and β-anomers of xylose.
evidence: Experimental findings reported in the manuscript

claim: The dual-activity LARGE enzyme is capable of extending products of B4GAT1.
source: The dual-activity LARGE enzyme is capable of extending products of B4GAT1 and we provide experimental evidence that B4GAT1 is the priming enzyme for LARGE.
evidence: Experimental findings reported in the manuscript

claim: B4GAT1 is the priming enzyme for LARGE.
source: The dual-activity LARGE enzyme is capable of extending products of B4GAT1 and we provide experimental evidence that B4GAT1 is the priming enzyme for LARGE.
evidence: Experimental findings reported in the manuscript

claim: B4GAT1 is involved in the initiation of the LARGE-dependent repeating disaccharide that is necessary for extracellular matrix protein binding to O-mannosylated α-dystroglycan.
source: Our results further define the functional O-mannosylated glycan structure and indicate that B4GAT1 is involved in the initiation of the LARGE-dependent repeating disaccharide that is necessary for extracellular matrix protein binding to O-mannosylated α-dystroglycan that is lacking in secondary dystroglycanopathies.

claim: The LARGE-dependent repeating disaccharide is lacking in secondary dystroglycanopathies.
source: Our results further define the functional O-mannosylated glycan structure and indicate that B4GAT1 is involved in the initiation of the LARGE-dependent repeating disaccharide that is necessary for extracellular matrix protein binding to O-mannosylated α-dystroglycan that is lacking in secondary dystroglycanopathies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results and prior knowledge

claim: Glycosylation is the most abundant and diverse post-translational modification of proteins.
source: Glycosylation is the most abundant and diverse post-translational modification of proteins (Varki, 2011).

claim: There are over 200 individual glycosyltransferases in humans.
source: The synthesis of complex glycans is catalyzed by the action of over 200 individual glycosyltransferases in humans (Moremen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moremen et al., 2012

claim: Glycosyltransferases exhibit exceptional selectivity for the donor sugar nucleotide and the underlying acceptor glycan as well as stereo- and linkage-specificity.
source: For most of the enzymes studied to date, there is exceptional selectivity for the donor sugar nucleotide and the underlying acceptor glycan as well as stereo- and linkage-specificity for the catalyzed additions (Moremen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moremen et al., 2012

claim: Mutations in genes encoding glycosyltransferases have been established as causal for a variety of human diseases including congenital muscular dystrophy.
source: Mutations in the genes encoding many of these glycosyltransferases have been established as causal for a variety of human diseases including congenital muscular dystrophy, specifically the secondary dystroglycanopathies (Barresi and Campbell, 2006; Freeze, 2007; Wells, 2013; Praissman and Wells, 2014).

claim: At least a dozen enzymes/proteins are involved in the synthesis of O-mannose-initiated glycans that when defective lead to various forms of congenital muscular dystrophy.
source: At least a dozen enzymes/proteins are involved in the synthesis of O-mannose-initiated glycans that when defective lead to various forms of congenital muscular dystrophy, termed secondary dystroglycanopathies, that range from the phenotypically mild Limb-Girdle to the severe Walker-Warburg muscular dystrophies (Muntoni et al., 2011; Mercuri and Muntoni, 2012; Dobson et al., 2013; Praissman and Wells, 2014).

claim: Secondary dystroglycanopathies range from the phenotypically mild Limb-Girdle to the severe Walker-Warburg muscular dystrophies.
source: At least a dozen enzymes/proteins are involved in the synthesis of O-mannose-initiated glycans that when defective lead to various forms of congenital muscular dystrophy, termed secondary dystroglycanopathies, that range from the phenotypically mild Limb-Girdle to the severe Walker-Warburg muscular dystrophies (Muntoni et al., 2011; Mercuri and Muntoni, 2012; Dobson et al., 2013; Praissman and Wells, 2014).

claim: Until recently, α-dystroglycan was the only well established O-mannoslyated mammalian protein.
source: Until recently (Lommel et al., 2013; Vester-Christensen et al., 2013; Winterhalter et al., 2013), α-dystroglycan, a central component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex that serves to connect the cytoskeleton inside the cell with the extracellular matrix outside the cell, was the only well established O-mannoslyated mammalian protein (Barresi and Campbell, 2006; Endo and Manya, 2006).

claim: α-dystroglycan is a central component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex that serves to connect the cytoskeleton inside the cell with the extracellular matrix outside the cell.
source: Until recently (Lommel et al., 2013; Vester-Christensen et al., 2013; Winterhalter et al., 2013), α-dystroglycan, a central component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex that serves to connect the cytoskeleton inside the cell with the extracellular matrix outside the cell, was the only well established O-mannoslyated mammalian protein (Barresi and Campbell, 2006; Endo and Manya, 2006).

claim: The proper O-mannosylation of α-dystroglycan is essential for its ability to bind to components of the extracellular matrix including laminin.
source: The proper O-mannosylation of α-dystroglycan is essential for its ability to bind to components of the extracellular matrix including laminin (Ervasti and Campbell, 1993; Barresi and Campbell, 2006).

claim: Mutations in B3GNT1 have been connected with congenital muscular dystrophies.
source: Recently, reports in the literature have connected mutations in B3GNT1 with congenital muscular dystrophies (Buysse et al., 2013; Czeschik et al., 2013; Shaheen et al., 2013) and specifically to the defective glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (Jae et al., 2013) even though no O-mannose glycan structures containing a β3-GlcNAc have yet to be elucidated (Praissman and Wells, 2014).

claim: Mutations in B3GNT1 have been connected specifically to the defective glycosylation of α-dystroglycan.
source: Recently, reports in the literature have connected mutations in B3GNT1 with congenital muscular dystrophies (Buysse et al., 2013; Czeschik et al., 2013; Shaheen et al., 2013) and specifically to the defective glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (Jae et al., 2013) even though no O-mannose glycan structures containing a β3-GlcNAc have yet to be elucidated (Praissman and Wells, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jae et al., 2013

claim: B3GNT1 (also known as iGnT) was reported in 1997 to be the first successfully cloned β-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase involved in the synthesis of poly-N-acetyllactosamine.
source: In 1997, B3GNT1 (also known as iGnT) was reported to be the first successfully cloned β-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase involved in the synthesis of poly-N-acetyllactosamine (Sasaki et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 1997

claim: Poly-N-acetyllactosamine chains consist of the repeating disaccharide -β3-GlcNAc-β4-Gal-.
source: Poly-N-acetyllactosamine chains consist of the repeating disaccharide -β3-GlcNAc-β4-Gal-, a structure termed the i-antigen when unbranched (Ujita et al., 2000; Zhou, 2003).

claim: Unbranched poly-N-acetyllactosamine is termed the i-antigen.
source: Poly-N-acetyllactosamine chains consist of the repeating disaccharide -β3-GlcNAc-β4-Gal-, a structure termed the i-antigen when unbranched (Ujita et al., 2000; Zhou, 2003).

claim: Poly-N-acetyllactosamine is a prevalent glycan substructure found in N-glycans and O-glycans on proteins.
source: Poly-N-acetyllactosamine is a prevalent glycan substructure found in N-glycans and O-glycans on proteins whose abnormal levels have been associated with human diseases including cancer (Ujita et al., 2000; Zhou, 2003; Ho et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2014).

claim: Abnormal levels of poly-N-acetyllactosamine have been associated with human diseases including cancer.
source: Poly-N-acetyllactosamine is a prevalent glycan substructure found in N-glycans and O-glycans on proteins whose abnormal levels have been associated with human diseases including cancer (Ujita et al., 2000; Zhou, 2003; Ho et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2014).

claim: B3GNT2, B3GNT3 and B3GNT4 were cloned by Hennet's and Sasaki's groups.
source: Shortly thereafter, work carried out by Hennet's and Sasaki's groups led to the cloning of three other β-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases, B3GNT2, 3, and 4 (Zhou et al., 1999; Shiraishi et al., 2001).

claim: B3GNT2, B3GNT3 and B3GNT4 share motifs with β3-galactosyl-transferases as well as β3-GalNAc-transferases.
source: Importantly, B3GNT2, B3GNT3 and B3GNT4 were found to share motifs with β3-galactosyl-transferases as well as β3-GalNAc-transferases (Zhou et al., 1999; Shiraishi et al., 2001; Togayachi et al., 2006).

claim: B3GNT2, B3GNT3 and B3GNT4 are in the same Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes database (CAZy) family.
source: These three enzymes are in the same Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes database (CAZy) family and group together based on primary sequence similarity and motifs hypothesized to play a role in forming the β3 linkage (Zhou et al., 1999; Shiraishi et al., 2001; Togayachi et al., 2006).

claim: B3GNT1 lacks the motifs shared by B3GNT2, B3GNT3 and B3GNT4 and is in a different CAZy family.
source: B3GNT1 lacks these motifs and is in a different CaZY family, interestingly one shared with LARGE and LARGE2 that contain both xylosyl- and glucoronsyl–transferase activity and which functionally modify O-mannosylated glycans (Inamori et al., 2012; Goddeeris et al., 2013; Inamori et al., 2013).

claim: B3GNT1 is in the same CAZy family as LARGE and LARGE2.
source: B3GNT1 lacks these motifs and is in a different CaZY family, interestingly one shared with LARGE and LARGE2 that contain both xylosyl- and glucoronsyl–transferase activity and which functionally modify O-mannosylated glycans (Inamori et al., 2012; Goddeeris et al., 2013; Inamori et al., 2013).

claim: LARGE and LARGE2 contain both xylosyl- and glucoronsyl–transferase activity.
source: B3GNT1 lacks these motifs and is in a different CaZY family, interestingly one shared with LARGE and LARGE2 that contain both xylosyl- and glucoronsyl–transferase activity and which functionally modify O-mannosylated glycans (Inamori et al., 2012; Goddeeris et al., 2013; Inamori et al., 2013).

claim: LARGE and LARGE2 functionally modify O-mannosylated glycans.
source: B3GNT1 lacks these motifs and is in a different CaZY family, interestingly one shared with LARGE and LARGE2 that contain both xylosyl- and glucoronsyl–transferase activity and which functionally modify O-mannosylated glycans (Inamori et al., 2012; Goddeeris et al., 2013; Inamori et al., 2013).

claim: The B3GNT1 enzyme is a binding partner for LARGE in mammalian cells.
source: Furthermore, it has been reported that the B3GNT1 enzyme is a binding partner for LARGE in mammalian cells (Bao et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bao et al., 2009

claim: B3GNT1 does not transfer UDP-GlcNAc to Gal-β4-GlcNAc-β-pNP under the tested conditions.
source: Incubation of the purified protein with UDP-[3H]GlcNAc and an enzymatically synthesized and purified substrate, Gal-β4-GlcNAc-β-pNP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), under previously reported buffering conditions for B3GNTs (Zhou et al., 1999; Shiraishi et al., 2001) failed to result in a detectable product as measured by incorporation of radioactivity into substrate (Figure 1).

claim: B3GNT2 shows clear N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase activity toward the N-acetyllactosamine acceptor.
source: Side-by-side extended (overnight) incubations of B3GNT1 and the B3GNT2 enzyme preparations with acceptor and sugar nucleotide showed clear N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase activity toward the acceptor only with B3GNT2, as assayed by radioactive incorporation of GlcNAc into the N-acetyllactosamine acceptor (Figure 1, glycans displayed in symbolic representations [Varki et al., 2009]).

claim: B3GNT1 aligns strongly with LARGE and LARGE2 in the glucuronyltransferase domain DXD-motif region.
source: B3GNT1 aligned strongly with LARGE and LARGE2 in the glucuronyltransferase domain DXD-motif region typically involved in metal ion dependent sugar nucleotide binding.
evidence: Multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A

claim: The DXD-motif is typically involved in metal ion dependent sugar nucleotide binding.
source: B3GNT1 aligned strongly with LARGE and LARGE2 in the glucuronyltransferase domain DXD-motif region typically involved in metal ion dependent sugar nucleotide binding.

claim: The DXD-motif was shown to be necessary for the glucuronyltransferase activity of LARGE and LARGE2.
source: This DXD-motif was shown to be necessary for the glucuronyltransferase activity of LARGE and LARGE2 consistent with probable sugar nucleotide binding in this region (Inamori et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inamori et al., 2013

claim: B3GNT2 did not align well with B3GNT1 or the LARGE proteins.
source: B3GNT2 did not align well with B3GNT1 or the LARGE proteins (Figure 2A).
evidence: Multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A

claim: B3GNT1 transfers GlcA to α- and β-xylopyranosides.
source: Incubation of B3GNT1 and UDP-GlcA with multiple glycan acceptors resulted in significant transfer only to α- and β-xylopyranosides, as measured by radioactive transfer from UDP-[14C]GlcA (Figure 2B).

claim: B3GNT2 did not transfer GlcA to either anomeric form of xylopyranoside tested.
source: B3GNT2 did not transfer GlcA to either anomeric form of xylopyranoside tested (data not shown).
evidence: Experimental data mentioned but not shown

claim: LARGE transfers GlcA to α-xylopyranosides but not β-xylopyranosides.
source: Our results confirm previous reports that LARGE transfers GlcA to α-xylopyranosides but not β-xylopyranosides (Figure 2C, [Inamori et al., 2012, 2013]).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C and supported by citations

claim: B3GNT1 is not hampered by the stereochemistry of the acceptor sugar.
source: In contrast, B3GNT1 does not appear to be hampered by the stereochemistry of the acceptor sugar (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2C

claim: Soluble forms of B3GNT1 and LARGE do not form a complex in vitro.
source: Following re-purification of LARGE based on the epitope tag, we were unable to detect the presence of B3GNT1 suggesting that the soluble forms of the proteins do not interact in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: B3GNT1 has a Km value of 3.0 mM for α-xylopyranoside as an acceptor.
source: We performed kinetic analysis of B3GNT1 and LARGE using the α-xylopyranoside as an acceptor and determined only minor differences (3.0 and 6.0 mM, respectively) in Km values for the acceptor (Table 1).

claim: LARGE has a Km value of 6.0 mM for α-xylopyranoside as an acceptor.
source: We performed kinetic analysis of B3GNT1 and LARGE using the α-xylopyranoside as an acceptor and determined only minor differences (3.0 and 6.0 mM, respectively) in Km values for the acceptor (Table 1).

claim: At 2 mM UDP-GlcA, B3GNT1 has a specific activity that is 48 times higher than LARGE for α-xylopyranoside as the acceptor.
source: However, at 2 mM UDP-GlcA, B3GNT1 has a specific activity that is 48 times higher than LARGE for α-xylopyranoside as the acceptor (Table 1).

claim: B3GNT1 has a Km value of 4.0 mM for β-xylopyranoside as an acceptor.
source: For B3GNT1, we were also able to use β-xylopyranoside as an acceptor and determined that the enzyme was more than twice as efficient with this acceptor as opposed to its anomer, α-xylopyranoside, though the Km value for the acceptor (4.0 mM) was only slightly altered (Table 1).

claim: B3GNT1 is more than twice as efficient with β-xylopyranoside as an acceptor compared to α-xylopyranoside.
source: For B3GNT1, we were also able to use β-xylopyranoside as an acceptor and determined that the enzyme was more than twice as efficient with this acceptor as opposed to its anomer, α-xylopyranoside, though the Km value for the acceptor (4.0 mM) was only slightly altered (Table 1).

claim: B3GNT1 possesses a significantly higher specific activity, turnover rate and catalytic efficiency than LARGE toward the monosaccharide α-xylopyranoside acceptor.
source: Thus, B3GNT1 possesses a significantly higher specific activity, turnover rate and catalytic efficiency than LARGE toward the monosaccharide α-xylopyranoside acceptor and is even more efficient with the β-anomer that LARGE is not able to utilize (Table 1).

claim: B3GNT1 is a xylopyranoside β1,4-glucuronyltransferase.
source: From this analysis, we determined that B3GNT1 is a xylopyranoside β1,4-glucuronyltransferase that we designate, using standard convention, B4GAT1 and, as previously described, we confirmed that LARGE contains xylopyranoside β1,3- glucuronyltransferase activity (Inamori et al., 2012).
evidence: NMR data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: LARGE contains xylopyranoside β1,3-glucuronyltransferase activity.
source: From this analysis, we determined that B3GNT1 is a xylopyranoside β1,4-glucuronyltransferase that we designate, using standard convention, B4GAT1 and, as previously described, we confirmed that LARGE contains xylopyranoside β1,3- glucuronyltransferase activity (Inamori et al., 2012).
evidence: NMR data shown in Figure 3 and supported by citation

claim: LARGE can extend GlcA-β4-Xyl-α-pNP (a product of B4GAT1) with α3-linked xylose.
source: Reactions were carried out overnight at 37°C with UDP-Xyl as the donor. Substrates and products were desalted by reverse phase C18 spin columns and then subjected to C18 reverse-phase HPLC. Distinct substrate and product peaks were detected for each of the three potential acceptors tested and the identity of each peak was confirmed by LC-MS/MS (Figure 4).

claim: LARGE can extend GlcA-β4-Xyl-β-MU (a product of B4GAT1) with α3-linked xylose.
source: Reactions were carried out overnight at 37°C with UDP-Xyl as the donor. Substrates and products were desalted by reverse phase C18 spin columns and then subjected to C18 reverse-phase HPLC. Distinct substrate and product peaks were detected for each of the three potential acceptors tested and the identity of each peak was confirmed by LC-MS/MS (Figure 4).

claim: LARGE can extend GlcA-β3-Xyl-α-pNP (its own disaccharide product) with α3-linked xylose.
source: Hence, LARGE can extend both disaccharide products of B4GAT1 and its own disaccharide product with α3-linked xylose.

claim: LARGE produces tetrasaccharide products from all three tested trisaccharides when incubated with UDP-GlcA.
source: Incubation of the trisaccharides with UDP-GlcA and LARGE produced tetrasaccharide products in all cases, which were observed by HPLC and confirmed by LC-MS/MS (Figure 5).

claim: B4GAT1 was unable to produce any observable tetrasaccharide using any of the three trisaccharides as acceptors.
source: In sharp contrast, we were unable to produce any observable tetrasaccharide with B4GAT1 using any of the three trisaccharides as acceptors (Figure 5), though the enzyme was active for transfer to monosaccharide xylopyranosides (Figure 2).

claim: B4GAT1 and LARGE do not possess branching activity toward disaccharides containing a terminal GlcA residue.
source: We tested whether B4GAT1 or LARGE were capable of transferring glucuronic acid to any of the tagged purified disaccharides GlcA-β4-Xyl-α-pNP, GlcA-β4-Xyl-β-pNP or GlcA-β3-Xyl-α-pNP. We did not detect any transfer of GlcA in these in vitro assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: B4GAT1 rapidly completes transfer to substrate.
source: B4GAT1 rapidly completes transfer to substrate. ∼1200 DPM represents complete transfer to the 10 nmol of substrate present.

claim: LARGE is unable to transfer to Xyl-β-pNP.
source: LARGE is unable to transfer to Xyl-β-pNP (Figure 6B) and shows a significant lag in initial transfer to Xyl-α-pNP before the formation of polymer.

claim: LARGE shows a significant lag in initial transfer to Xyl-α-pNP before the formation of polymer.
source: LARGE is unable to transfer to Xyl-β-pNP (Figure 6B) and shows a significant lag in initial transfer to Xyl-α-pNP before the formation of polymer.

claim: B4GAT1 and LARGE together demonstrate robust initial transfer activity and formation of polymer using either Xyl-α-pNP or Xyl-β-pNP as substrate.
source: In contrast, B4GAT1 and LARGE together demonstrate robust initial transfer activity and formation of polymer using either substrate.

claim: Extensive polymerization is achievable following incubation with both B4GAT1 and LARGE.
source: Analysis of the synthesized polymer via mass spectrometry shows extensive polymerization is achievable following incubation with both enzymes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: LARGE possesses poor initiating activity but works efficiently in polymer formation once B4GAT1 is added for initial transfer of GlcA.
source: These data provide further evidence that LARGE possesses poor initiating activity but works efficiently in polymer formation once B4GAT1 is added for initial transfer of GlcA.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data in Figure 6

claim: A phosphorylated O-mannose trisaccharide (core M3) attached to α-dystroglycan and its extension by LARGE is directly involved in the required ECM ligand binding activity.
source: A phosphorylated O-mannose trisaccharide (core M3, [Praissman and Wells, 2014]) attached to α-dystroglycan and its extension by LARGE after poorly defined intermediate biosynthetic steps (Figure 7) has been shown to be directly involved in the required ECM ligand binding activity (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010; Inamori et al., 2012; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).

claim: The specific activity and catalytic efficiency of B4GAT1 towards the tested monosaccharide xylosides is greater by more than an order of magnitude compared to LARGE catalysis.
source: Since we have shown that the specific activity and catalytic efficiency of B4GAT1 towards the tested monosaccharide xylosides is greater by more than an order of magnitude compared to LARGE catalysis (Table 1), this suggests that B4GAT1 is an initiating enzyme for LARGE-dependent glycan synthesis.

claim: B4GAT1 is an initiating enzyme for LARGE-dependent glycan synthesis.
source: Since we have shown that the specific activity and catalytic efficiency of B4GAT1 towards the tested monosaccharide xylosides is greater by more than an order of magnitude compared to LARGE catalysis (Table 1), this suggests that B4GAT1 is an initiating enzyme for LARGE-dependent glycan synthesis.

claim: B4GAT1 serves exclusively as a priming enzyme.
source: It also appears that B4GAT1 serves exclusively as a priming enzyme since we could not detect B4GAT1 modification of LARGE extended trisaccharides (Figure 5).
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data in Figure 5

claim: There is only one type of repeating disaccharide (Xyl-α3-GlcA-β3) attached to α-dystroglycan that is synthesized by LARGE.
source: This leads to the conclusion that there is only one type of repeating disaccharide (Xyl-α3-GlcA-β3) attached to α-dystroglycan that is synthesized by LARGE.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data showing no branching

claim: Neither LARGE nor B4GAT1 is capable of adding GlcA to a disaccharide that has been capped with GlcA, suggesting that branching is not occurring.
source: We also demonstrate that neither LARGE nor B4GAT1 is capable of adding GlcA to a disaccharide that has been capped with GlcA suggesting that branching is not occurring (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: At least one of the remaining incompletely characterized genes implicated in functional glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (FKTN, FKRP, ISPD, and TMEM5) likely encodes a xylosyltransferase to provide a substrate for B4GAT1.
source: In sum, our data provide a basis for further attempts to fully elucidate the functional LARGE-dependent O-mannose-initiated structure(s) and suggests that at least one of the remaining incompletely characterized genes implicated in functional glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (FKTN, FKRP, ISPD, and TMEM5, [Jae et al., 2013; Wells, 2013]) likely encodes a xylosyltransferase to provide a substrate for B4GAT1.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data and prior knowledge

claim: B4GAT1 is essential for proper glycosylation of α-dystroglycan.
source: Given that B4GAT1 is essential for proper glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (Bao et al., 2009; Buysse et al., 2013; Czeschik et al., 2013; Shaheen et al., 2013) and that LARGE is incapable of transferring GlcA to a β-xylopyranoside (Figure 2, [Inamori et al., 2012, 2013]) or generating a polymer from pNP-β-Xyl without B4GAT1 present (Figure 6), our findings strongly suggest that the underlying xylose is in a β-linkage on α-dystroglycan.

claim: The underlying xylose is in a β-linkage on α-dystroglycan.
source: Given that B4GAT1 is essential for proper glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (Bao et al., 2009; Buysse et al., 2013; Czeschik et al., 2013; Shaheen et al., 2013) and that LARGE is incapable of transferring GlcA to a β-xylopyranoside (Figure 2, [Inamori et al., 2012, 2013]) or generating a polymer from pNP-β-Xyl without B4GAT1 present (Figure 6), our findings strongly suggest that the underlying xylose is in a β-linkage on α-dystroglycan.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data and citations

claim: Deficiencies in B4GAT1 are associated with loss of functional glycosylation and laminin binding of α-dystroglycan and are causal for congenital muscular dystrophy.
source: This work also clarifies why deficiencies in this enzyme would be associated with loss of functional glycosylation and laminin binding of α-dystroglycan and be causal for congenital muscular dystrophy (Bao et al., 2009; Buysse et al., 2013; Czeschik et al., 2013; Shaheen et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data and supported by citations

claim: Loss of expression of B4GAT1 (B3GNT1), similar to loss of expression of LARGE, can lead to loss of laminin-binding α-dystroglycan and promote metastasis in certain cancers.
source: Further, our results likely clarify how loss of expression of B4GAT1 (B3GNT1), similar to loss of expression of LARGE (de Bernabe et al., 2009), can lead to loss of laminin-binding α-dystroglycan and promote metastasis in certain cancers (Bao et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data and supported by citations

claim: B4GAT1 has previously been observed to be in complex with B4GALT1, an enzyme required for poly-N-acetyllactosamine synthesis.
source: For example, B4GAT1 has previously been observed to be in complex with B4GALT1, an enzyme required for poly-N-acetyllactosamine synthesis (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009

claim: Similarities exist between HS (and other proteoglycan) biosynthesis pathways and the LARGE-dependent functional O-mannose glycan assembly pathway built on α-dystroglycan.
source: Similarities exist between HS (and other proteoglycan) biosynthesis pathways and the LARGE-dependent functional O-mannose glycan assembly pathway built on α-dystroglycan (Figure 7).
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison of pathways

claim: Both HS and the functional O-Man structure contain non-reducing end repeating disaccharides.
source: Included in these similarities are that they both contain non-reducing end repeating disaccharides (GlcA and GlcNAc for HS and GlcA and Xyl for the functional O-Man structure), they both contain an acidic glycan (GlcA), there is a copolymerase that has dual–enzymatic activity (exostoses enzymes for HS and LARGE for the functional O-Man glycan structure), both require a specific underlying core structure, and each contains specific priming glycosyltransferases (EXTLs for HS [Kitagawa et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2001], B4GAT1 for the functional O-Man glycan structure) that adds one of the sugars found in the repeat to the underlying core structure to initiate elongation.
